title: Hexagonal & Clean Architecture
summary: Named architectural styles that formalize the same boundary-and-dependency-direction rules — a core with no outward dependencies, surrounded by adapters — and where each name's vocabulary comes from.

slides.markdown:
[Dependency inversion](dependency-inversion-and-boundaries) showed one inverted dependency between a business layer and a database. Hexagonal architecture and Clean Architecture take that exact same idea — a core defining interfaces, outer code implementing them — and apply it as an organizing principle for an **entire application**, not just at the database boundary.

They're not really two different techniques competing for your allegiance. They're two names, drawn by two different authors (Alistair Cockburn and Robert C. Martin), for the same shape: a dependency-free core surrounded by rings or hexagon faces of infrastructure. Interviewers use both terms interchangeably more often than you'd expect, and knowing that they're the same idea under different vocabulary is itself a useful signal to project.

slides.subTitle: A core with no outward dependencies, surrounded by adapters
slides.markdown:
Strip away the naming differences and every one of these styles makes the same claim: put your application's actual reason for existing — the business rules — in a **core** that has zero dependencies on anything outside it. No web framework import, no ORM import, no cloud SDK import.

Everything the core needs from the outside world — a database, an email service, a message queue, the clock — it expresses as an interface it owns (a port, from the [previous topic](dependency-inversion-and-boundaries)). Everything that talks to the core from the outside — an HTTP handler, a CLI command, a scheduled job — also goes through a port.

The practical test: could you run the core's tests with the web framework, the database driver, and the cloud SDK all uninstalled? If the core module doesn't even reference their packages, the answer is yes.

slides.subTitle: Ports and adapters around an application core
slides.markdown:
Alistair Cockburn's version draws the core as a hexagon — the shape has no special meaning, it's just chosen to have room for several faces, since real applications need more than two ports (unlike a simple top/bottom layered diagram).

Each face of the hexagon is a port. Driving ports are called by the outside world to make the application do something (an HTTP controller calling a use case). Driven ports are called by the application to reach something it needs (a repository interface). Adapters plug into each face from outside: a REST adapter and a CLI adapter both driving the same use cases through the same port; a Postgres adapter and an in-memory-test adapter both satisfying the same repository port.

slides.subTitle: Entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks
slides.markdown:
Robert C. Martin's version draws the same idea as concentric rings instead of a hexagon, with four named rings from center outward:

1. **Entities** — the innermost ring. Enterprise-wide business rules and objects, the ones that would be true even without this specific application.
2. **Use cases** — application-specific business rules; the orchestration of entities to accomplish one thing a user wants ("place an order", "approve a refund").
3. **Interface adapters** — converters: controllers, presenters, gateways that translate between use cases and the outside world's formats.
4. **Frameworks & drivers** — the outermost ring. Web frameworks, databases, UI toolkits — the "details."

<<< Image: four concentric circles, innermost labelled Entities, then Use Cases, then Interface Adapters, then outermost Frameworks & Drivers, with a single arrow crossing all four rings from outside to inside labelled "Dependency Rule: source code dependencies point only inward" >>>

slides.subTitle: Source code dependencies point only inward
slides.markdown:
Clean Architecture states the rule the hexagon only implies visually: **source code dependencies can only point inward.** Nothing in an inner ring can name anything in an outer ring — not a class, not a function, not even a constant.

This is the same rule as dependency inversion, restated at the scale of an entire application rather than one database call. When an inner ring needs something from an outer one — a use case needs to persist an entity — it defines an interface in the inner ring and lets the outer ring implement it. That's the same port-defined-on-the-inside pattern, applied uniformly at every ring boundary, not just the database one.

Crossing the boundary at runtime (a controller calling a use case) is fine and expected. Crossing it at the *source-dependency* level in the wrong direction is the one thing the whole architecture exists to prevent.

slides.sectionTitle: Hexagonal vs. onion vs. Clean Architecture
slides.subTitle: Same core idea, different vocabulary
slides.markdown:
| Style | Author | Shape | Core term |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters** | Alistair Cockburn | Hexagon with faces | Application core, ports, adapters |
| **Onion Architecture** | Jeffrey Palermo | Concentric rings | Domain model at the center |
| **Clean Architecture** | Robert C. Martin | Concentric circles | Entities, use cases |

All three agree on the substance: an inner region with no outward dependencies, an outer region holding "details" (frameworks, databases, UI), and a strict rule that dependencies point inward only. They disagree mainly on naming and on how many named rings to draw.

In practice, teams often say "hexagonal" and mean "Clean Architecture" and vice versa, and an interviewer rarely penalizes mixing the vocabulary as long as you can explain the actual mechanism — the inward-only dependency rule — correctly.

The **use case** ring (also called "application services" or "interactors") is where a lot of the actual value of this style shows up day to day. A use case is a class or function representing one thing an actor wants to accomplish — `PlaceOrder`, `ApproveRefund`, `CancelSubscription` — and its job is purely **orchestration**: pull an entity via a port, ask it to do something, save the result via another port.

The use case itself contains no business rule about *whether* an order is valid — that logic lives in the entity (`Order.canBeCancelled()`). It contains no SQL — that lives behind a repository port. What it contains is the sequence: check preconditions, call the entity, persist, publish an event. This separation is why use cases tend to read almost like plain English when written well, and why they're the easiest place in the whole architecture to unit test — a handful of mocked ports and one entity.

slides.sectionTitle: What lives at the outermost ring
slides.subTitle: Frameworks, DB drivers, UI — the "details"
slides.markdown:
Calling the outermost ring "details" is a deliberate provocation. It means your choice of web framework — Express, Spring, Django — is, architecturally, a *detail*. So is your choice of database, your ORM, your message broker, your UI toolkit.

This isn't saying these choices don't matter for building the system — they obviously do. It's saying they shouldn't matter to the *core business logic*, which should be describable, and testable, without naming any of them. A useful gut check: could you explain what your use case does to a non-technical domain expert without mentioning a single product name (Postgres, Kafka, React)? If yes, the use case is probably clean. If the explanation is full of vendor names, the details have leaked into the core.

The most common criticism of this style, and a fair one: applying its full ceremony to a small CRUD app. A four-ring structure with entities, use cases, interface adapters, and gateways for a service that does nothing but validate a form and insert a row means writing five files and three interfaces to accomplish what a single 15-line function would do just as correctly.

The telltale sign this has happened: a use case class whose entire body is `repository.save(mapper.toEntity(request))`, with no actual business rule anywhere in it — pure ceremony, zero payoff, because there's no rule complex enough to be worth protecting from the framework.

The fix isn't to abandon the idea, it's to right-size it: apply the full ring structure where business logic genuinely has rules worth isolating, and let a thin CRUD endpoint stay thin. A later topic in this group, Architectural Boundaries in Practice, covers exactly how to make that call.

slides.sectionTitle: A minimal use case, in code
slides.markdown:
The shape stays small even in a real example — orchestration only, no framework names, no SQL.

```python
# use_cases/cancel_subscription.py
class CancelSubscription:
    def __init__(self, subscriptions: SubscriptionRepository, clock: Clock, events: EventPublisher):
        self.subscriptions = subscriptions
        self.clock = clock
        self.events = events

    def execute(self, subscription_id: str) -> None:
        subscription = self.subscriptions.find_by_id(subscription_id)
        if subscription is None:
            raise SubscriptionNotFound(subscription_id)

        subscription.cancel(at=self.clock.now())   # business rule lives on the entity
        self.subscriptions.save(subscription)
        self.events.publish(SubscriptionCancelled(subscription_id))
```

`SubscriptionRepository`, `Clock`, and `EventPublisher` are all ports. Nothing here names Postgres, Stripe, or Kafka — a test can construct this use case with three in-memory fakes and assert `subscription.status == "cancelled"` with no I/O at all.

Hexagonal and Clean Architecture answer *where the boundary goes* and *which direction dependencies point*. They deliberately say very little about **how to model what's inside the core** — how to represent an order, a subscription, or a customer as objects with real behavior instead of data bags.

That's the gap Domain-Driven Design fills, and it's why the two ideas show up together constantly in practice: DDD's entities, value objects, and aggregates are exactly what tends to live inside the innermost ring of a Clean Architecture diagram or the core of a hexagon. The next few topics in this group pick up that thread.
